fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says he “…did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit.” (2 Kings 14:24) Same name, same road. Two Jeroboams, and this one walks the first Jeroboam's road.

Yes, baker. The text calls him “…His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.” (2 Kings 14:25) The LORD spoke a word through him, and King Jeroboam's borders came back just as that word said. The word came first, and the borders followed.

Gaza, baker? You went shopping in the wrong neighborhood! The text says Jeroboam “…waged war and recovered both Damascus and Hamath for Israel…” (2 Kings 14:28) Damascus is the one that fills the blank. Gaza doesn't show up in these verses.

Nice try, friend, but the text doesn't mention any trading. It says “the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there.” (2 Kings 15:4) The high places were not taken away, and sacrificing and burning incense are what the people kept doing.

Training soldiers isn't what the text says, baker. It says “the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there.” (2 Kings 15:4) Sacrificing and burning incense is what the people kept doing at the high places.

That's it, baker. The text says Zechariah “…did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done.” (2 Kings 15:9) He did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit. So the text puts him in line with his fathers.

The text doesn't say he was worse, friend. It says he “…did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done.” (2 Kings 15:9) That's how the text compares him to his fathers. It never says he went further than they did.

Four, baker. Right after Zechariah's reign ends, the text says the word of the LORD spoken to Jehu was fulfilled: “Four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” (2 Kings 15:12) The LORD said four, and the text says it happened. What the LORD says comes true.

Gold, baker? Somebody's been watching too many treasure movies! The text says “…Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver…” (2 Kings 15:19) Pul is the king of Assyria, and silver is what the verse names. Gold from the palace isn't mentioned.

Fighting men aren't who the text names, friend. It says Menahem “…exacted this money from each of the wealthy men of Israel…” (2 Kings 15:20) The wealthy men are the ones asked for fifty shekels of silver each. The king of Assyria gets the silver.

Yes, baker. The text says Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, “…took the people as captives to Assyria.” (2 Kings 15:29) He captures places like Gilead, Galilee and all the land of Naphtali first. That's a heavy verse, and I think it hurts.

Yes, baker. The text says Hoshea son of Elah “…attacked Pekah, killed him, and reigned in his place.” (2 Kings 15:30) That's the same pattern we've seen over and over in this passage: a conspiracy, a king struck down, and a new king in his place. So True is the answer, and the text says it plainly.

That's right, baker. The text says, “In those days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.” (2 Kings 15:37) Pekah is the king of Israel from earlier in this passage. So the LORD begins sending Israel's king and Aram's king against Judah.

Hoshea isn't named in this verse, friend. In it, “…the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.” (2 Kings 15:37) Hoshea is the man who conspired against Pekah, so Pekah is the name that fits the blank.
